pages.text: An expression calculates a value from literals, variables, constants and operators. It always ends with an OPERATOR block showing $(1);$(). An expression may go on in the next line, one block further east.
Calculations follow the usual rules: $(1)*$() before $(1)+$(). Use $(1)($() and $(1))$() to group. A division with $(1)/$() always gives a FLOAT.

A minus sign in front of a name or a $(1)($() turns the sign around: $(1)- x * 2 ;$(). The minus sign is an OPERATOR block of its own, so the text notation writes $(1)- x$(), not $(1)-x$(). $(1)-7$() in one piece is a LITERAL with a negative number.

Some rules are less usual. $(1)\$() binds weaker than $(1)*$() and $(1)/$(): $(1)7 \ 3 * 2$() is $(1)7 \ 6$(), so use parentheses. $(1)⊕$() binds weaker than $(1)+$(), and AND binds tighter than OR: $(1)a OR b AND c$() means $(1)a OR ( b AND c )$().
You can't call a function inside an expression. Use a CALL statement instead.
